sourceBindings.text: A lower maize leaf turns yellow. Where is the yellowing: along its centre, along its edges, or between its veins? Describe what you actually see before deciding what may have caused it. A photograph is a clue, not a fertilizer instruction.
Match nine N, P and K name, function and symptom cards with reasons; distinguish maize N midrib V-yellowing, K margin yellowing and older-leaf Mg interveinal striping.
At each station, record the crop, plant part, position and age of affected leaves and the visible pattern before a qualified hypothesis; state a plausible alternative cause.
Choose field observations and a suitable soil or crop-stage-specific tissue test to check a hypothesis, without calculating or prescribing fertilizer from a picture.

sourceBindings.text: A lower maize leaf has yellow outer edges but a greener centre. A second lower leaf has a yellow V along the central vein.
Describe the visible route and leaf age for each before choosing a label.
K is the stronger hypothesis for the first leaf; N for the second. The shared older-leaf position alone cannot distinguish them.
Check whether the patterns recur across the field, inspect roots and water conditions, then use appropriate tests before management.
The location of yellowing is evidence; neither photograph is a complete diagnosis.

sourceBindings.text: Young maize is small and purplish after a cold, wet week; soil P status is not yet known.
P shortage is plausible from the colour and growth pattern, but not established.
Cold, wet soil and reduced root activity can limit P uptake even when soil P is sufficient.
Inspect root condition and weather; interpret soil P and, if useful, appropriately sampled tissue results before deciding on treatment.
A visually plausible nutrient label must survive alternative explanations.

sourceBindings.text: chlorosis
Loss of normal green colour, often visible as yellowing.
deficiency
An inadequate nutrient supply or use relative to plant needs; a symptom alone does not prove it.
leaf margin
The outer edge of a leaf.
midrib
The main central vein of a leaf.
stunted
Growing smaller or more slowly than expected for that crop and stage.
interveinal chlorosis
Yellowing between veins while the veins stay greener.
internal remobilization
Redistribution of a nutrient from older tissues toward newer tissues after uptake.

sourceBindings.text: Individually groups all nine cards into three justified N/P/K sets and identifies the N centre-V, K outer-margin yellowing and P young-maize purpling patterns on the checked station images. Magnesium interveinal striping is optional enrichment, not an additional core pass requirement.
Pass only with all three justified card matches and pattern distinctions correct. A wrong function or symptom receives targeted feedback and an open retry.

For at least one N, one P and one K image, separates direct observation from a likely explanation, records whether affected leaves are older or newer, and offers a plausible non-nutrient or uptake-related alternative.
Pass when all three records use the visible evidence and at least one alternative is reasoned; colour alone or an unqualified diagnosis does not pass.
For the cool-soil purple maize case and an edge-yellowing case, explains which field context to check and when soil and/or suitably sampled tissue analysis could help confirm nutrient status.
Pass when the learner states the limits of visual diagnosis and does not prescribe a fertilizer or rate from an image; otherwise review and retry.
